chapter_theme: Under the heading தெரிந்து தெளிதல், thirteen verses on examining before trusting or acting: the giver who does not weigh the asker, the witness who weighs even what he saw, the go-between caught in a quarrel, the near small gain over the far large one, water taken for shallow, the loser who suspects even gods, fair-seeming dependants who rob, and private scrutiny joined to going with the town.

183.reading: The one who ruled the world, thinking the gift easy for him, poured the gift-water lavishly without knowing the measure of the one who had come to him, and lost it all, for those who begin a thing with a flaw in it there is no affliction that they have not brought on themselves.
183.nuance: The heavy lengthenings (ஆஅம், மேஎம், தோஒம், தாஅம்) give the verse its sound. The ruler pours water (நீர் பெய்து) as a giver seals a gift; his fault is not giving but giving without weighing the recipient, so the verse fits its heading as trust given without examination.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no affliction that does not come of one's own giving

story.act: a ruler of the world, sure the gift was easy for him, poured the gift-water without knowing who had come and lost his world
story.tradition: by tradition the king Mahabali, who granted three steps to Vishnu in dwarf form; the verse names only one who ruled the world

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the gift-giver who does not weigh the asker brings his ruin on himself

184.reading: Even kin of good quality speak without weighing their words, so there is no point in grieving at the want of good nature in those not of good family, lord of the land where cascades stir on the rock, for there is no one at all who never slips in speech.
184.nuance: The argument runs from the greater to the less: if the well-born slip, the lapse of the low-born is no wonder. The verse assumes that good family (இற்பாலர்) yields good nature, and then uses that assumption to excuse rather than to condemn.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no one whoever who does not falter in speech

story.act: no story; a general claim about every speaker

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one should not grieve over another's careless words, since even the good let words slip

185.reading: When the king asked men to show the boundary marks of the land of Pukar of cool flowering waters, the worthy man, ashamed of what he had come to hold, kept it hidden, and so even what one has seen with one's own eyes is to be weighed before it is spoken.
185.nuance: The episode is compressed and its point is unclear: கொண்டதனை may be what the worthy man had taken or accepted, or what he had grasped of the matter. On either reading the proverb's lesson is that eyewitness alone does not license speech.
185.domain_note: a witness questioned by the king

pazhamozhi.literal: even what is seen with the eyes should be spoken after thought

story.act: a king of Pukar asked men to show a land's boundary marks and a worthy man, from shame, concealed what he knew

pazhamozhi.applied_to: testimony, even of what one saw, needs weighing before it is given

186.reading: If, in a quarrel that has flared between two who rose in anger without understanding, someone enters between them out of friendship, the two in their great hatred turn on him and he is caught in the knot at the head of the fight.
186.nuance: The mediator is not blamed for malice but for misjudging the moment: the two have not understood (உணராது), and a friend's entry turns both angers on him. குறுக்கண்ணி is a rare word; it is taken as a cross-knot or tie in which the go-between is caught.

pazhamozhi.literal: he becomes the cross-knot at the head

story.act: no story; the go-between in a quarrel

pazhamozhi.applied_to: stepping between two who quarrel without understanding draws the anger of both

187.reading: Better to take what is close at hand though it be only a millet-grain's worth than to get however much from far away, lord of the cloud-ringed hills where herds of stags tear the honeycombs, for no one eats the palmyra's fruit by planting the palm.
187.nuance: The palmyra takes many years to bear, so the planter does not live to eat the fruit; the proverb weighs gain by its distance in time as well as space.

pazhamozhi.literal: people do not eat the palmyra's fruit by planting it
pazhamozhi.applied_to: a small gain near at hand is to be preferred to a large one far off

188.reading: The verse says that even when they have set their heart on it people do not do what is unfitting, that what has been spoken with weight must be kept, and that one should do even what one would not do if it pleases one's people, for no one ever impaled his own kin.
188.nuance: The proverb names the king's harshest punishment, impalement (கழுவேற்றல்), and says it is never turned on one's own people; the counsel to please the people even at some cost to oneself follows from that bond. Lines 1-3 are three loosely joined counsels, and how they lead to the proverb is not certain.
188.domain_note: one who holds power over his people

pazhamozhi.literal: no one has ever impaled his own kin

story.act: no story; the punishment of impalement, never inflicted on one's own

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one bears with and pleases one's own people rather than treat them as enemies

189.reading: A man whose head was painfully split, who lost the use of his legs as well, who was dubbed 'the walking duck' and with his lameness got another name, shows why people do not go into water taking it for shallow.
189.nuance: The cost the verse dwells on is not the injury alone but the new name it brings, a lasting mockery. நடைத்தாரா is taken as 'walking duck', a nickname for a waddling lame man; the episode behind it is not told.

pazhamozhi.literal: people do not go in, taking the water to be shallow

story.act: a man who plunged into water thinking it shallow split his head, was lamed and was nicknamed the walking duck

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one should not enter on anything before testing its depth

190.reading: Those who have attached themselves to the wealthy, getting at first a little gruel, will get a large portion too, for if a man gets a place to sit in a crowded space, he will get a place to lie down as well.
190.nuance: The verse is a counsel of patient entry, not of greed: the small first share is the foothold. அரிதாம் இடத்துள் makes the space hard to get, so the first seat is what counts.
190.domain_note: one who attaches himself to a wealthy patron

pazhamozhi.proverb: இடத்துள் ஒருவன் இருப்புழிப் பெற்றால் கிடப்புழியும் பெற்று விடும்
pazhamozhi.literal: one who gets room to sit will get room to lie down too

story.act: no story; a seat in a crowded place grows into a bed

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a small first share from the wealthy grows into a large one

191.reading: Can those who truly discern mean speech from good speech live by the way of harsh speech, the verse asks, since mean speech brings a man into trouble, while sweet speech never puts anyone in danger.
191.nuance: The argument is from the speaker's safety, not the hearer's pleasure: knowing the two kinds of speech is enough to choose the sweet, because only the mean one rebounds on the speaker.

pazhamozhi.literal: sweet speech never brings one into trouble

story.act: no story; a claim about speech

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one who can tell good speech from mean will not choose harsh words

192.reading: Whether men enter openly being of true nature or bring their ends about being of false nature, let them be whatever they are; for each, to be true to his own nature is foremost.
192.nuance: The verse seems to set truth and falsehood side by side without choosing between them and to prize only constancy of nature; this may be a counsel to the observer to judge each man by his settled nature rather than his professions. The sense of விரியப் புகுவார் is not clear.

pazhamozhi.literal: being of one's own nature is foremost

story.act: no story; a maxim on keeping one's own nature

pazhamozhi.applied_to: whatever a man is, true or false, his constancy to his own nature is what counts

193.reading: Whoever they may be, those who have lost their property will suspect harm even of the gods, lady who appears like a painted doll, for one who has lost a long spear will search for it even inside a pot.
193.nuance: The proverb is comic: a long spear cannot be in a pot, yet loss drives the search everywhere. Under its heading the verse reads as a warning that a loser's suspicions are no proof against those he suspects.

pazhamozhi.literal: one who has lost a long spear searches even in a pot

story.act: no story; the absurd search for a lost spear

pazhamozhi.applied_to: loss makes a man suspect everyone, even the gods

194.reading: Taking clothes and food in the hours of sleep, coming into view when the sunlight spreads, and showing themselves as though they were attached to one, lady of spear-like eyes, there are thieves like peacocks.
194.nuance: The peacock is a figure of a fair outside; the thieves are fair-seeming dependants who rob by night and appear devoted by day, so the danger is inside the household's own circle. The image is not explained beyond the comparison.

pazhamozhi.literal: the world has thieves who are like peacocks

story.act: no story; dependants who steal by night and appear loyal by day

pazhamozhi.applied_to: those who seem close may be the ones who rob

195.reading: The verse says not to go away so that those attached to one are left desolate, not to stay on departing from the path of those who renounced, and to examine again and again the fine point one has seen for oneself, without hearing others, and to run along with the town's way.
195.nuance: The verse joins private, repeated scrutiny with outward conformity: examine for oneself, but act with the town. நீத்தார் may be those who have renounced or those who have left one, and line 2 is uncertain.

pazhamozhi.literal: run in step with the town's way

story.act: no story; a maxim of going with the community

pazhamozhi.applied_to: having examined for oneself, one acts in step with the community

links.note: Kural 510 says trusting without examining brings endless trouble; Pazhamozhi 183 gives the case of a ruler who gave without weighing the one who came and lost the world.
links.teaches: Together they show that the couplet's untested trust covers generosity too: the open-handed king who does not weigh the asker suffers the very trouble the Kural assigns to careless trust.
links.list_adds: its story turns the couplet's abstract fault into a royal gift, so the failure to examine is shown in the act the ethics books most praise, giving.

links.note: Kural 423 asks for the truth of whatever is heard from any mouth; the proverb of Pazhamozhi 185 asks that even what one saw be weighed before it is spoken.
links.teaches: The pair extends testing from what one hears to what one has seen and from judging to speaking: the Kural doubts others' report, the proverb doubts one's own eyes as a ground for testimony.
links.list_adds: it moves the test from the hearer's understanding to the witness's speech before a king, adding the shame that makes a worthy man hold back.

links.note: Both set the millet grain against the palmyra: in Kural 104 a millet-sized kindness is reckoned palm-sized, in Pazhamozhi 187 a millet-grain's gain near at hand is preferred and the palm is the tree too slow to feed its planter.
links.teaches: The same millet-and-palm scale serves two judgements of value: the Kural enlarges the small out of gratitude, Pazhamozhi prefers the small because it is near and certain, so the image teaches valuing the small for moral and for prudential reasons.
links.list_adds: it makes the palm stand for delay rather than size, adding time to a scale the couplet uses only for magnitude.

links.note: Kural 99 asks why one who sees the sweetness sweet speech yields would use harsh words; Pazhamozhi 191 asks the same of those who can tell good speech from mean, and answers that only mean speech brings trouble.
links.teaches: The two rest one choice on two motives: the Kural on the good that sweet speech brings, Pazhamozhi on the danger harsh speech brings back to the speaker, so the case for sweet speech is both gain and safety.
links.list_adds: its proverb turns the couplet's rhetorical question into a rule about risk, that sweet speech never endangers, which the couplet does not state.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 191 says sweet speech never brings anyone into trouble; Thirikadugam 24 names a courtesan's sweet words as a mire that sinks those who step in.
links.teaches: Read together they show the proverb holds for the speaker, not the hearer: one's own sweet speech is safe, but another's sweet speech may be bait, so sweet speech protects the one who uses it and can trap the one who trusts it.

links.note: Both close on உடைத்து, 'the world holds such': Kural 277 those bright outside like the kunri seed and black within, Pazhamozhi 194 thieves like peacocks who seem attached by day and rob by night.
links.teaches: Pazhamozhi moves the Kural's hidden-black ascetic into the household: the false outside belongs to dependants who live with one, and the betrayal is a theft of food and clothing in the hours of sleep.
links.list_adds: it gives the couplet's single colour image a sequence of acts, night theft and daylight show of attachment, which makes the deceit something one can watch for.

links.note: Thirikadugam 51 says deceivers stay deceivers even when they keep close and that examination shows them; Pazhamozhi 194 shows deceivers who keep close, appearing attached by day while stealing by night.
links.teaches: The pair says both that closeness proves nothing and what the examination must look for: the gap between the day's show of attachment and the night's acts.

links.note: Kural 426 says understanding lives as the world lives; Pazhamozhi 195 closes on running with the town's way, but first asks for repeated private scrutiny of what one has seen without heeding others.
links.teaches: The pair shows that going with the world is the end of a private test, not a substitute for it: Pazhamozhi puts one's own repeated examination before conformity, as the Kural's chapter sets 423 beside 426.
links.list_adds: it ranks the counsels in order, not abandoning dependants, not leaving the renouncers' path, examining for oneself, and only then conforming, so conformity comes last.

source_issues: 186 line 4: குறுக்கண்ணி is rare and the proverb's image cannot be fixed.
189 line 2: நடைத்தாரா is obscure; the episode behind the nickname is not told.
192 line 1: விரியப் புகுவார் is unclear, and the verse's stance on truth and falsehood is uncertain.
